title: Jio Is Filing for India's Biggest IPO Ever. None of Its Major Investors Plan to Sell.
excerpt: Reliance's telecom-to-AI arm is pitching a valuation of up to $170 billion. Meta, Google and KKR are staying in. Every rupee raised goes straight into the company — and India's second half is about to absorb more than $15 billion in new listings.
body:
India's IPO Pipeline Has Never Looked Like This

Reliance Jio Platforms is preparing to file for what could become the largest initial public offering in Indian market history, and it has chosen a moment when Indian capital markets are about to absorb an unprecedented wave of new listings.

According to Reuters, Jio held talks with its 13 marquee foreign investors — including Meta, Google, KKR, Vista Equity Partners and three Gulf sovereign wealth funds — about selling down roughly 8 per cent of their individual stakes. The effective free float would be about 2.5 per cent of Jio's total outstanding shares, which at the valuation investment bankers have been pitching — up to $170 billion — would make even this modest offering one of the largest in Indian history.

Here is the striking detail: none of the big investors are planning to exit. Every rupee raised will go directly into the company.

## What Jio Wants to Become

Most Indians still think of Jio as the company that gave them cheap data. It has over 500 million telecom subscribers. But the IPO prospectus, when it arrives, will tell a different story.



> **"JP Morgan recently called this domestic buying power "structural" and predicted it would outlast the foreign selling cycle."**


Jio is spending aggressively on AI infrastructure, cloud computing, enterprise software and data centres. At Reliance's annual general meeting, chairman Mukesh Ambani framed the company's future around three pillars: AI, digital services and physical retail technology. Meta and Reliance announced a $100 million joint venture for AI. Google agreed to establish a dedicated cloud region in Jamnagar, Gujarat, for Reliance's operations.

The bet is that Jio's telecom network — the largest in India — becomes the rails on which a much larger technology business runs. If investors buy that thesis, Jio's valuation leapfrogs from a telecom multiple (typically 8–12 times EBITDA) into technology territory (20–30 times or higher).

"Jio is not being fully valued within Reliance's broader petrochemicals and retail portfolio, and a separate listing would help unlock higher value for the telecom and digital unit," Saurabh Parikh, a senior analyst at ICRA, told Reuters.

## The Second Half Is Packed

Jio is not alone. The National Stock Exchange — India's dominant trading venue — has also filed its draft papers, reportedly targeting ₹30,000 crore ($3.6 billion). SBI Mutual Fund, India's largest asset manager, is lined up for a ₹10,000 crore ($1.2 billion) offering. Quick-commerce darling Zepto is planning a roughly $500 million Mumbai listing. PhonePe, the country's biggest digital payments app, filed a confidential prospectus with SEBI earlier this year.

Add them up and the second half of 2026 could see more than $15 billion in primary issuances hit the Indian market — a figure that would rival any six-month stretch in the country's capital-markets history.

The timing is not accidental. Indian retail investors have been absorbing record foreign outflows — more than $30 billion year-to-date — through systematic investment plans that now channel over ₹25,000 crore a month into mutual funds. JP Morgan recently called this domestic buying power "structural" and predicted it would outlast the foreign selling cycle.

## The NRI Investor Question

For the diaspora, India's IPO boom has historically been a spectator sport. Regulatory complexity, FEMA compliance, and the mechanics of NRI demat accounts have kept many overseas Indians on the sidelines while domestic retail investors have had first access.

That may be changing. Jio's listing, if it reaches the scale being discussed, would be large enough to attract dedicated NRI tranches and make brokers actively court diaspora capital. The RBI's recent move to make dollar deposits in Indian banks more attractive — with hedged yields around 6–7 per cent — signals a broader push to bring NRI money back into Indian financial instruments.

The question for NRI investors is not whether Jio is a good company. It plainly is. The question is whether a $170 billion valuation for a company that still derives most of its revenue from telecom subscriptions — in a market where average revenue per user is under $3 a month — prices in the AI and cloud pivot before it has materialised.

Ambani first flagged plans to list Jio in 2019, promising an IPO within five years. It has taken seven. The delay, if nothing else, suggests that even Reliance wanted the business to mature before facing the scrutiny of public-market investors. When the filing drops — Reuters reports it could be as early as this month — it will be the most closely watched document in Indian corporate history.

Whether the IPO marks the beginning of India's technology coming-of-age or the peak of its AI valuation fever will depend on what Jio actually delivers with the money it raises. The investors who are not selling seem to think it is the former.
